entities.summary:
The Battle of the Somme was a pivotal and bloodiest battle of World War I, fought between British and French forces against the German army between 1 July and 18 November 1916. The battle took place in the Somme River valley in northern France, near the city of Albert. It was one of the deadliest battles in human history, with over 1 million casualties, including more than 400,000 British soldiers who lost their lives. The battle marked a significant turning point in the war, as it weakened the German army and paved the way for the Allied victory in 1918.

The battle was a culmination of months of planning and preparation by the British military, which had been trying to break through the German defenses along the Somme River. The British army launched a massive assault on 1 July 1916, with over 1,000 tanks and artillery pieces, but the attack was met with fierce resistance from the German army. The battle raged on for months, with both sides suffering heavy casualties.

The Battle of the Somme had a profound impact on the course of World War I and the world at large. It led to a significant shift in the balance of power in Europe and marked a turning point in the war. The battle also had a lasting impact on the lives of soldiers and civilians, with many suffering from physical and emotional trauma.

The Battle of the Somme remains a powerful symbol of the horrors of war and the sacrifices made by soldiers and civilians during World War I. It continues to be remembered and commemorated today, with many visiting the Somme to pay their respects to the fallen soldiers.

The battle's legacy continues to be felt today, with many of the soldiers who fought in the battle going on to play important roles in shaping the course of history in the years that followed. The battle's impact on the world at large was significant, with many of the soldiers who fought in the battle returning home to become prominent figures in politics, literature, and the arts.
